analysis.investment_thesis: Abram Food fails the Magic Formula's core test: ROE of 0.52% signals near-zero return on capital, so even a cheap-looking P/E of 10.6 is meaningless. A "cheap" company that doesn't earn a decent return on its capital is a value trap, not a bargain.
key_strengths: P/E of 10.6 is optically cheap versus FMCG peers
Promoter holding of 67.33% shows skin in the game
Asset-light agro-trading model can theoretically scale
key_risks: ROE of 0.52% implies negligible return on capital — fails Magic Formula
Tiny 32.5 Cr microcap with limited disclosure and liquidity
Commodity agro-trading offers no moat or pricing power
red_flags: ROE <1% — capital is being deployed with essentially zero productivity
Earnings/equity mismatch suggests recent IPO cash dilution or weak core economics
Undifferentiated 'other food products' business in a commodity segment
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies on earnings yield AND return on capital — a business must be both cheap and good. Abram Food clears the first bar only weakly (P/E 10.6 ≈ earnings yield ~9.4%, below my 12% threshold once you adjust for enterprise value) and fails the second bar dramatically. A 0.52% ROE is effectively a company earning nothing on its capital base — far below the 20%+ ROIC I look for. No amount of cheapness compensates for capital that doesn't compound.

The ROE vs. market cap math also hints at data quality problems (likely a recent IPO with fresh cash bloating the denominator), which is itself a reason for a quant approach to skip the name — the Magic Formula works best on seasoned businesses with clean, multi-year EBIT histories. Commodity agro-trading at sub-1% ROE, in a 32.5 Cr microcap with no disclosed EBIT margin, operating cash flow, or capex profile, is exactly the kind of name the systematic screen should filter out. Avoid.
